title.en: The Charge of Illegitimacy: How the Judgment Hall Got Its Name
title.zh: 非婚生之訟：審判廳得名之由

region.en: The Hall of the Two Truths, Egyptian Other World

texts.period: Doctrine reconstructed from the Metternich Stele and Pyramid Texts (Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I, 1911)

source.work: E. A. W. Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection, vol. I (1911), ch. III, the charge of illegitimacy and the Hall of the Two Truths

summary.en: Why the Hall of Judgment is called the Hall of the Two Truths: Set had tried to seize his brother's widow and accused Isis of playing the harlot and Horus of illegitimacy; at the trial before the gods Thoth declared Osiris 'true of word', Isis by implication 'true of voice', and she and her sister were ever after present at the judgment of the dead bearing the title 'Ladies (i.e., possessors) of the Truth.'
summary.zh: 審判之廳何以稱『雙真理之廳』：塞特欲奪兄嫂不遂，遂訟伊西斯為娼、荷魯斯為非婚生；諸神庭前，托特既判奧西里斯『言真實』，伊西斯亦因之為『言真實』者——自此姊妹常侍亡者之審判，佩『真理之主』之榮號，而其廳遂名『雙真理之廳』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient theology reconstructed via Budge 1911; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Set, it seems, had shut her up in some building, but she effected her escape, and fled to the city of Buto (Pe-Tep) in the Delta. There in the papyrus swamps she brought forth Horus, and there she reared him unknown to anyone.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Osiris and the Egyptian Resurrection vol. I (1911), ch. III, from the Metternich Stele narrative.

passages.text: With the Egyptian accounts of the begetting of Horus before us, we are right in assuming that Set brought a charge of illegitimacy against Horus, and that his accusations were levelled as much against Isis as against her son. The text of the Metternich Stele suggests that Set had tried to seize his brother's widow for himself, and it states quite clearly that she escaped from the place wherein he had managed to confine her for a time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

passages.text: Isis and her sister Nephthys were present at the trial before the gods, the latter presumably as a witness, and Thoth having declared that Osiris had spoken the truth, Isis was by implication also declared 'true of word,' or 'true of voice,' and she and her sister were ever after present at the judgment of the dead, and they bore the honourable title of 'Ladies (i.e., possessors) of the Truth,' and the Hall of Judgment became known as the 'Hall of the two Truths.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1911), ch. III.

title.en: The Origins of the Resurrection: Graves of Predynastic Egypt
title.zh: 復活信仰之源：前王朝埃及墓葬

region.en: Nakadah and the prehistoric graves of Upper Egypt
region.zh: 埃及上埃及納卡達與史前墓群

texts.period: Predynastic burials (c. 6000-3500 BCE); doctrine traced in Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. V

source.work: Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life, by E. A. W. Budge (1899), ch. V, 'The Resurrection and Immortality'

summary.en: Where the whole Egyptian hope of rising began: the three kinds of predynastic graves — bodies laid on the left side in the ante-natal position wrapped in gazelle skin ('the symbol of a hope that as the child is born from this position into the world, so might the deceased be born into the life in the world beyond the grave'); bodies stripped and jointed; bodies burnt — each with offerings of food and flint weapons: 'The man who would hunt and fight in the next world must live again.'
summary.zh: 埃及復活之望所自始：前王朝三類墓葬——其一，屍左臥屈肢如胎兒，裹以羚羊皮（『如嬰兒自是位而生於世，願亡者亦如是生於彼界』）；其二，剝肉剔骨；其三，焚屍——然皆隨葬食物與燧石兵器：『欲於來世獵而戰者，必先得再生。』

sensitivity.note: Archaeological doctrine via Budge 1899; no living community restrictions. Budge's 'ante-natal position' reading is his own inference.

passages.text: In the oldest tombs we find the skeleton laid upon its left side, with the limbs bent: the knees are on a level with the breast, and the hands are placed in front of the face. Generally the head faces towards the south, but no invariable rule seems to have been observed as to its orientation. Before the body was laid in the ground it was either wrapped in gazelle skin or laid in loose grass... In burials of this class there are no traces of mummification, or of burning, or of stripping the flesh from the bones.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. V.

passages.text: Now in all classes of tombs belonging to the prehistoric period in Egypt we find offerings in vases and vessels of various kinds, a fact which proves beyond all doubt that the men who made these graves believed that their dead friends and relatives would live again in some place, of the whereabouts of which they probably had very vague ideas, in a life which was, presumably, not unlike that which they had lived upon earth. The flint tools, knives, scrapers and the like indicate that they thought they would hunt and slay their quarry when brought down, and fight their foes... The man who would hunt and fight in the next world must live again; and if he would live again it must be either in his old body or in a new one; if in the old body, it must be revivified.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. V.

passages.text: The former are buried in the ante-natal position of a child, and we may perhaps be justified in seeing in this custom the symbol of a hope that as the child is born from this position into the world, so might the deceased be born into the life in the world beyond the grave; and the presence of amulets, the object of which was to protect the body, seems to indicate that they expected the actual body to rise again. The latter, by the mutilation of the bodies and the burning of the dead, seem to show that they had no hope of living again in their natural bodies.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1899), ch. V.

texts.language: Archaeological evidence (no text); Egyptian funerary doctrine
texts.canonical_translation: E. A. W. Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (London, 1899), ch. V

narrative.en:
Egypt's grandest idea — that the dead rise — did not begin with a text but with a grave. In the oldest burials of Upper Egypt, at Nakadah and other prehistoric sites, the skeleton is laid upon its left side with the knees at the breast and the hands before the face, wrapped in gazelle skin or loose grass: the ante-natal position of a child. There are no inscriptions (writing was unknown), but there are offerings in vases, flint knives for the hunt, and schist amulets against invisible enemies — everything a dead man would need to live, hunt, and fight again.

Budge's argument, from the evidence of three burial customs, is that the earliest Egyptians already held two distinct theologies of the corpse. The first kind of grave — the crouched, unmutilated body — belongs to people who expected the actual body to rise: born once from the foetal position, born again from the grave in the same body, revivified. The second kind — bodies stripped of flesh, bones cast in wild confusion or 'jointed' to save space, sometimes with the head separated, sometimes burnt — belongs to people who seemingly had no hope of living again in the natural body, and whose conception of a resurrection, if any, must have been of a spiritual body only. The third kind marks the transition: clay casings over folded bodies.

What the dynastic Egyptians then did was to reverse the second custom and universalize the first. By the 4th Dynasty every funerary text assumes the body will be buried whole — a reversal to which we owe the great anti-decay spells ('O flesh of Pepi, rot not, decay not, stink not') and, in time, the whole apparatus of embalming, the Ka statues, the Book of the Dead, and the promise of Osiris: that the god who had been a mortal and had risen from the dead would make his followers rise likewise. The belief in a future life, Budge concludes, is older than the belief in God as Egypt formulated it: its beginnings must be as old as the oldest human remains found in the valley — traces of bitumen on prehistoric bones showing that the attempt to preserve the dead, and the hope it embodied, was there at the very beginning.

THE DATING QUESTION. Budge is careful about chronology: the interval between these graves and the reign of Mena, the first historical king, 'must have been very considerable', representing thousands of years — yet the beliefs handed on through that interval were not wiped out and were scarcely modified, surviving 'in an almost unchanged state at the latest period of Egyptian history'. Even the College of Heliopolis, editing the ancient funeral texts, did not dare to delete the savage allusions their ancestors had written: objectionable passages were merely softened or left, out of 'their own reverence for the written word'. The theology of the resurrection was thus, in the strictest sense, prehistoric — older than the dynasty, older than writing, older than the gods as Egypt named them; and the later religions of Osiris and of Ra did not invent it but inherited it, clothing an immemorial grave-hope in ever more splendid garments.

functions: Documentary origin of the resurrection doctrine: burial customs as the pre-textual theology of rising
Etiology of embalming: the reversal of predynastic mutilation-customs explains the whole-body doctrine of the dynastic age
Social anthropology of the grave: offerings, weapons and amulets as the equipment of a life expected to continue

variants.name: The dynastic whole-body doctrine
variants.text_tradition: Pyramid Texts and early funerary inscriptions
variants.summary: By the 4th Dynasty all texts assume burial of the body whole, reversing the predynastic mutilation customs — the doctrinal basis of embalming and the Ka statue.

variants.name: The bitumen traces
variants.text_tradition: Predynastic human remains from Egypt (de Morgan, Ethnographie Prehistorique, 1897)
variants.summary: The oldest human remains found in Egypt bear traces of bitumen, showing that the attempt to preserve the dead was made at the very beginning of settlement in the valley.

primary_sources.work: Predynastic burials at Nakadah and other Upper Egyptian sites
primary_sources.citation: Excavations reported in J. de Morgan, Ethnographie Prehistorique (Paris, 1897), p. 189; synthesized in Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life (1899), ch. V.

secondary_sources.work: E. A. W. Budge, Egyptian Ideas of the Future Life
secondary_sources.citation: Budge 1899, London: Kegan Paul — the classic statement of the argument from grave-types to doctrine.

title.en: Euhemerus and His Letters of Gold: Plutarch Refuses to Humanize the Gods
title.zh: 優赫莫魯斯與其金書：普魯塔克拒神化為人

region.en: Alexandria and the Panchaean letter of gold (the debate over the gods' nature)
region.zh: 亞歷山大城與潘凱亞金書（神祇性質之辯）

texts.period: Recorded by Plutarch, De Iside 23 (Budge translation 1912)

source.work: Legends of the Gods, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1912), Plutarch, The History of Isis and Osiris, sec. XXIII

summary.en: Plutarch's warning against the historians who bring gods down to earth: 'It would be to shake and loosen a worship and faith which have been firmly settled in nearly all mankind from their infancy... and to give a clear sanction to the impostures of Euhemerus the Messenian, who from mere imagination... has invented a new mythology of his own, asserting that all those in general who are called and declared to be gods are none other than so many ancient generals and sea-captains and kings' — found, he claimed, written in letters of gold in a country that no one else has ever visited.
summary.zh: 普魯塔克警告將神拽落人間之史家：『此乃動搖並鬆弛自人類嬰年即深植之崇拜與信仰……且授偽造者以明據——優赫莫魯斯憑空捏造新神譜，斷言凡所謂神者，無非古之將軍、舵師與君王』——其所據者，乃一無人曾至之國中『以金字書成』之文。

sensitivity.note: Ancient polemic via Plutarch; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: But I am much afraid that to give in to this explanation of the story will be to move things which ought not to be moved; and not only, as Simonides says, 'to declare war against all antiquity,' but likewise against whole families and nations who are fully possessed with the belief in the divinity of these beings. And it would be no less than dispossessing those great names of their heaven, and bringing them down to the earth.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Legends of the Gods (1912), Plutarch sec. XXIII.

passages.text: It would be to shake and loosen a worship and faith which have been firmly settled in nearly all mankind from their infancy. It would be to open a wide door for atheism to enter in at, and to encourage the attempts of those who would humanize the divine nature. More particularly it would give a clear sanction and authority to the impostures of Euhemerus the Messenian, who from mere imagination, and without the least appearance of truth to support it, has invented a new mythology of his own, asserting that 'all those in general who are called and declared to be gods are none other than so many ancient generals and sea-captains and kings.'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXIII.

passages.text: Now, he says that he found this statement written in the Panchaean dialect in letters of gold, though in what part of the globe his Panchaeans dwell, any more than the Tryphillians, whom he mentions at the same time with them, he does not inform us. Nor can I learn that any other person, whether Greek or Barbarian, except himself, has ever yet been so fortunate as to meet with these imaginary countries.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1912), Plutarch sec. XXIII.

title.en: The Riddle of the Hall: 'Whose Heaven Is Fire, Whose Walls Are Serpents?'
title.zh: 廳中之謎：『孰有天如火、牆為蛇者？』

region.en: The Hall of Truth, Egyptian Other World (symbolic pin, Abydos region)
region.zh: 埃及冥界真理之廳（象徵定位，阿拜多斯一帶）

texts.period: Book of the Dead ch. 125, final scene (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. IV, the closing riddle of the Great Judgment

summary.en: The last obstacle in the Hall of Truth: even the justified soul must answer the gate-keeper's riddle before entering — Thoth asks him, 'Who is he whose heaven is fire, whose walls are serpents, and the floor of whose house is a stream of water?' — and the deceased replies 'Osiris', and is bidden to advance; the priest's magic, Budge notes, thrusts itself 'into the most sacred of texts' at this point.
summary.zh: 真理之廳最後一關：縱屬義者，入內之前亦須應門者之謎——托特問曰：『孰有天如火、牆為蛇、其屋之地基為流水者？』——亡者答曰『奧西里斯』，遂蒙召而進；伯奇按：祭司之魔法於此處亦『插入最神聖之文』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary scene via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: One would think that the moral worth of the deceased was such that he might then pass without delay into the most holy part of the Hall of Truth where Osiris was enthroned. But this is not the case, for before he went further he was obliged to repeat the magical names of various parts of the Hall of Truth; thus we find that the priest thrust his magic into the most sacred of texts. At length Thoth, the great Recorder of Egypt, being satisfied as to the good faith and veracity of the deceased, came to him and asked why he had come to the Hall of Truth, and the deceased replied that he had come in order to be 'mentioned' to the god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. IV.

passages.text: Thoth then asked him, 'Who is he whose heaven is fire, whose walls are serpents, and the floor of whose house is a stream of water?' The deceased replied, 'Osiris'; and he was then bidden to advance so that he might be introduced to Osiris. As a reward for his righteous life sacred food, which proceeded from the Eye of Ra, was allotted to him, and, living on the food of the god, he became a counterpart of the god.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. IV.

title.en: Behold, I Am in Thy Presence: Ani Becomes a Spirit-Body
title.zh: 看哪，我立於爾前：阿尼化為靈體

region.en: The Kingdom of Osiris, Egyptian Other World
region.zh: 埃及冥界奧西里斯之國

texts.period: Papyrus of Ani, 18th Dynasty (c. 1400-1300 BCE); trans. Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VII

source.work: The Book of the Dead, by E. A. Wallis Budge (1901), ch. VII, the judgment scenes of the Papyrus of Ani

summary.en: The verdict of the scales, in the words of the vignette: 'I have come to thee, Un-Nefer, I have brought to thee the Osiris Ani. His heart is righteous and hath come forth from the Balance. It hath no sin before any god or any goddess. Thoth hath set down his judgment in writing, and the Company of the Gods have declared on his behalf that [his] evidence is very true' — and Ani answers: 'Behold, I am in thy presence, O Lord of Amentet. There is no sin in my body. I have not uttered a lie knowingly... Grant that I may be like the favoured (or rewarded) ones who are in thy train.' Under favour of Osiris Ani then became a sahu, or 'spirit-body.'
summary.zh: 天秤判詞之畫銘：『我來就爾，安-奈菲爾；我攜奧西里斯-阿尼以來。其心正直，自天秤而出；於諸神之前無罪。托特筆錄其判，諸神團為之證言其實。』——阿尼答曰：『看哪，我立於爾前，阿門特之主。我身無罪。我未明知故言謊……願我如爾行列中蒙恩之人。』——蒙奧西里斯之恩，阿尼遂化為『靈體』（sahu）。

sensitivity.note: Ancient funerary vignette text via Budge 1901; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: I have come to thee, Un-Nefer, I have brought to thee the Osiris Ani. His heart is righteous [and] hath come forth from the Balance. It hath no sin before any god or any goddess. Thoth hath set down his judgment in writing, and the Company of the Gods have declared on his behalf that [his] evidence is very true. Let there be given unto him of the bread and beer which appear before Osiris. Let him be like the Followers of Horus for ever!
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, The Book of the Dead (1901), ch. VII (the words of the gods over Ani).

passages.text: Next we see Ani kneeling in adoration before Osiris, and he says, 'Behold, I am in thy presence, O Lord of Amentet. There is no sin in my body. I have not uttered a lie knowingly. [I have] no duplicity. Grant that I may be like the favoured (or rewarded) ones who are in thy train.' Under favour of Osiris Ani then became a sahu, or 'spirit-body,' and in this form passed into the Kingdom of Osiris.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1901), ch. VII.

title.en: Burning Apep in Wax: The Daily Rites of Banishing the Serpent
title.zh: 焚蠟製阿波菲斯：日日驅蛇之儀

region.en: The temple of Amen-Ra at Thebes (where the Book of Overthrowing Apep was performed)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯阿蒙-拉神廟（行滅阿波菲斯之書處）

texts.period: Ptolemaic copy of a far older liturgy, BM Papyrus 10188 (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. VI, the rites of the Book of Overthrowing Apep

summary.en: The daily war against the serpent, fought in wax and fire: when the sun-god arrived at the place of Apep he 'first of all cast a spell upon the monster, which rendered him helpless, and then he cast his fiery rays upon him, which shrivelled him up, and the fire of the god consumed him entirely'; in the temple the priests recited the spells that helped the god, 'burnt waxen figures of the monster in specially prepared fires, and, uttering curses, they trampled them under foot and defiled them' — rites believed also to break up rain clouds, scatter fog and mist, and dissipate thunder-storms.
summary.zh: 以蠟與火日日征蛇：日神至阿波菲斯處，『先以咒縛之使其無力，繼以火焰之射灼之，神火遂盡焚其身』；廟中祭司誦咒助神，『於特備之火中焚蠟製蛇像，口出咒詛，踐踏而污之』——此儀亦信能破雨雲、散霧靄、消雷暴。

sensitivity.note: Ancient execration liturgy via Budge 1910; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: This work is a liturgy, which was said at certain times of the day and night in the great temple of Amen-Ra at Thebes, with the view of preventing the monster Aapep from obstructing the sunrise. Aapep was supposed to lie in wait for the sun daily just before sunrise, with the view of doing battle with him and overthrowing him. When the Sun-god arrived at the place where Aapep was, he first of all cast a spell upon the monster, which rendered him helpless, and then he cast his fiery rays upon him, which shrivelled him up, and the fire of the god consumed him entirely.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Literature of the Ancient Egyptians (1910), ch. VI.

passages.text: In the temple of Amen-Ra the priests recited the spells that were supposed to help the Sun-god to burn up Aapep, and they burnt waxen figures of the monster in specially prepared fires, and, uttering curses, they trampled them under foot and defiled them. These spells and burnings were also believed to break up rain clouds, and to scatter fog and mist and to dissipate thunder-storms, and to help the sun to rise on this world in a cloudless sky. Aapep was a form of Set, the god of evil of every kind, and his allies were the 'Red Fiends' and the 'Black Fiends,' and every power of darkness.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. VI.

title.en: The House of Leto Carved from a Single Stone

region.en: Buto, Nile Delta, Egypt (the oracle enclosure of Leto)
region.zh: 埃及三角洲布托（雷托神諭聖域）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories II.155 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book II, sec. 155

summary.en: The marvel that made Herodotus marvel most at Buto: 'There is in this sacred enclosure a house of Leto made of one single stone as regards both height and length, and of which all the walls are in these two directions equal, each being forty cubits; and for the covering in of the roof there lies another stone upon the top, the cornice measuring four cubits.'
summary.zh: 希羅多德於布托最嘆為奇者：『聖域中有一雷托之室，高廣皆由整石鑿成，四面等長，各四十肘；其頂則以一石覆之，簷廣四肘。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient travel-wonder via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. The house sheltered the oracle and the floating island of Chemmis nearby.

passages.text: This Oracle which is in Egypt is sacred to Leto, and it is established in a great city near that mouth of the Nile which is called Sebennytic, as one sails up the river from the sea; and the name of this city where the Oracle is found is Buto... In this Buto there is a temple of Apollo and Artemis; and the temple-house of Leto, in which the Oracle is, is both great in itself and has a gateway of the height of ten fathoms: but that which caused me most to marvel of the things to be seen there, I will now tell.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book II.155.

passages.text: There is in this sacred enclosure a house of Leto made of one single stone as regards both height and length, and of which all the walls are in these two directions equal, each being forty cubits; and for the covering in of the roof there lies another stone upon the top, the cornice measuring four cubits.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book II.155.
